newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan weak money demand seen pre-empting rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan weak money demand seen pre-empting rate cut.

text.p: Economists on Tuesday said solid February money supply growth showed money demand remained weak, leaving little room for Taiwan's central bank to ease liquidity despite fears that a hog disease outbreak would slow growth.
Taiwan's broadest money supply measure, M2, grew 9.88 percent in February from the year-earlier period, the central bank said on Tuesday.
The growth figure was calculated by the central bank under a broader, revised definition of M2 measure introduced in January that analysts say adds 1.0 to 1.5 percentage points.
The February rise put M2 growth within the central bank's 9-14 percent target zone, but below an average 10.07 percent forecast in a March 21 Reuters poll of economists.

Economists said that left little room for the central bank to loosen monetary policy despite fears that an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease among the nation's hogs would shave a half percentage point from the 1997 economic growth rate.

"Now is not the time for the central bank to cut banks' reserve requirements because demand for money is still weak and liquidity is already relatively loose at the moment," said economist Stephen Wang of HSBC James Capel.

Economists noted that loans and investments grew just 8.12 percent year-on-year in February, slower than January's 8.63 percent rise, showing that a slow economic recovery was generating little new money demand even before the hog crisis.
The central bank had repeatedly pledged to cut Taiwan's bank reserve requirements at an unspecified "appropriate time" because they were high compared with other countries.

With inflation under control and M2 growth relatively sluggish, economists said businesses and investors were keen to know if the central bank would loosen liquidity to help the economy weather the disease's impact.
The Council of Agriculture on March 20 banned all pork exports and ordered the slaughter of all pigs, even healthy ones, at affected farms.
Central bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong said on Monday the crisis could reduce Taiwan's gross domestic product by half a percentage point in 1997.

Despite calls by legislators to loosen monetary policy to shield the economy's fragile recovery, Sheu said there would be no immediate change in the bank's "stable-to-loose, but not too loose" monetary policy.

Core Pacific economist J.C. Yang said: "From the economic point of view the central bank will not cut reserve requirements for the moment because money demand is not expected to rise significantly until June when the recovery turns clearer."
"But the central bank might face heavy political pressure to cut reserve requirements if the hog disease really affects the economy seriously," Yang said.
Economists said the central bank likely would loosen monetary policy gradually if a recent stocks rally fizzles.

Before the pork crisis sent stocks tumbling on March 21, share prices had surged for months to a six-year peak on March 18 -- prompting the central bank to issue billions of dollars in short-term paper to soak up liquidity that many experts said was fuelling the rise.
The new situation could prompt a reverse strategy.
"Now, as it (the central bank) must boost the economy due to the hog crisis, it should gradually ease its policy," said Grand Cathay Securities vice-president Terry Chen.
"The central bank will likely inject funds through open market operations, but not cut reserve requirements unless it faces further changes," Chen said.
